newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Investors take profits in coffee, metals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Investors take profits in coffee, metals.

text.p: Prices for coffee and base metals were hit by a wave of selling from nervous investors on Monday.
Coffee's fall was particularly severe at more than $350 a tonne as speculators took profits while a sell-off in industrial metals was led by a $50 drop in the price of copper.
London's robusta coffee futures tumbled in early trade on Monday with benchmark July hitting $2,100, a sharp $370 reverse from Friday's close. This compares with the recent 20-month-peak of $2,670.
The slide followed a steep 12-percent fall in New York on Friday on frantic speculative selling.

A sell-off in the New York market, which has been the leader for most of this year's moves, on Friday and again in early trade Monday, took some of the air out of the most spectacular bubble in the coffee market in 20 years.

"It's foolish to think a market goes in only one direction," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "When it rises that much, the pullbacks are going to be more severe. Moves like this take your breath away."
Coffee's run-up since early January was fuelled by depleting consumer and producer stocks, supply problems from Colombia and expectations of a lower Brazilian harvest.
A winter frost in Brazil in the coming weeks could also dent supply prospects from the world's largest grower. June and July are the frost danger months.
In industrial metals speculators appeared to be dumping some of their holdings as the market neared the traditionally slower offtake period during the Northern Hemisphere summer months.

A tentative settlement of a labour contract at the 110,000 tonnes a year nickel/90,000 tonnes copper Ontario facilities of Canadian producer Inco removed the the threat of a strike and helped trigger selling late Friday.

Copper prices on the London Metal Exchange dipped below $2,500 which triggered further selling down to $2,475 and nickel, used extensively in the production of stainless steel, plunged $250 a tonne to $6,950.

"The Inco (tentative) settlement removed quite a prop from the nickel market and with the peak shipping period for exports from Russian Arctic circle producers already on us there's not much reason to stay in this market," one analyst said.
Among other metals aluminium pierced an important support area around $1,600 and traders were looking for further selling.

News that Russia's platinum group metals export agency Almazjuvelirexport will be able to resume exports to Japan, the world's number one importer of platinum and palladium, after a six-month delay knocked prices slightly.
Platinum closed $2 lower at $402 an ounce and palladium $6.50 down at $172.50.
